question: Compare the performance of our Jeans category against Shorts and explain the difference.
sql:
SELECT p.category,
       COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id) AS orders,
       SUM(oi.sale_price) AS revenue,
       ROUND(AVG(oi.sale_price), 2) AS avg_selling_price,
       ROUND(AVG(p.retail_price), 2) AS avg_list_price,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price - p.cost), 2) AS gross_margin,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price - p.cost) / NULLIF(SUM(oi.sale_price),0) * 100, 1) AS margin_pct,
       ROUND(1 - AVG(oi.sale_price)/NULLIF(AVG(p.retail_price),0), 3) AS avg_discount_rate,
       SUM(CASE WHEN oi.status = 'Returned' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / NULLIF(COUNT(*),0) AS return_rate
FROM `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.order_items` oi
JOIN `bigquery-public-data.thelook_ecommerce.products` p ON p.id = oi.product_id
WHERE p.category IN ('Jeans','Shorts')
GROUP BY p.category
analyst_report: Revenue alone will mislead you on product comparisons. The four-way decomposition that explains almost every category gap is: units sold, average selling price, discount depth (1 - ASP/list), and return rate. A category can out-earn another on revenue while destroying margin through discounting - Jeans typically carries a higher list price but also a deeper discount rate. Always report gross margin AND margin %, because the absolute favours the bigger category and the percentage favours the smaller one; executives need both to allocate shelf space.
analyst_method_notes: Cost lives on products.cost; margin = order_items.sale_price - products.cost.
Discount depth = 1 - (sale_price / retail_price). This is the usual culprit.
Return rate must come from order_items.status, not orders.status.
